summary: Astro Health AI is a health companion that lets astronauts monitor their own health when Earth is minutes away. Each day the crew member logs eight indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, SpO2, glucose, sleep, mood, radiation) plus exercise. The app maps them onto a body twin and rates each one OK, Watch, Act or Critical using published clinical ranges, the astronaut's own baseline and recent trend. It detects multi-signal patterns such as a possible infection, gives a 48-hour early warning before problems peak, tracks radiation against NASA's 600 mSv career limit, and includes an assistant that explains every flag and tells the crew when and how to contact Earth from the ISS, the Moon or Mars. It matters because on deep-space missions the crew must catch problems early and act before Earth can answer.
details:
What it does

  • Daily check-in for 8 indicators plus an exercise log, with reading context (just woke up, after exercise, after EVA) and a morning/evening/weekly routine with streaks.
  • Body twin: each body zone (head, lungs, heart, abdomen, whole body, muscles and bones, chest dosimeter) shows its reading and status; tap a zone for its trend, explanation and follow-up actions.
  • Three checks per reading: clinical range (AHA/ACC, CDC, WHO, ADA, AASM/SRS), "unusual for you" against the pre-flight baseline, and "trending worse".
  • Pattern detection: possible infection or immune stress, possible breathing or oxygen problem, possible fluid loss or fainting risk, each with clear actions.
  • 48-hour early warning: a model trained on a research-based synthetic crew flags an infection or fluid-loss episode building up before the rules fire. It never changes a status; it is labeled as a warning, not a diagnosis.
  • Location-aware escalation for ISS, Moon and Mars (Mars: messages take up to about 20 minutes one way, so self-care steps come first).
  • Astro Health AI assistant: answers questions such as "Do I need to contact Earth?" from the app's own facts; built-in guidance works offline.
  • Alerts and a summary report for the flight surgeon; radiation dose tracked against the NASA-STD-3001 career limit (600 mSv).
  • Sources page: every threshold and model is listed with its source.

How we validated it Real day-by-day astronaut vitals are privacy-protected, so we built a research-based synthetic crew in which every parameter is traced to a published study, NASA document or real dataset, and checked that it reproduces published numbers (for example in-flight systolic blood pressure of about 106 mmHg, Circulation 2019, and ISS sleep of about 6.1 h, Barger 2014). On a test crew the model never saw (20 synthetic people), the early warning flagged 32 of 40 infections and 18 of 20 fluid-loss episodes before their peak, versus 6 and 7 for the rules alone, with warnings on 1.8% of normal days. This shows the software behaves as designed; clinical validation needs real astronaut data.

Benefits Explains every flag in plain language, personal baselines instead of one-size-fits-all, honest about uncertainty, and built for crews who must act on their own.

What we hope to achieve A crew-facing early-warning tool for Moon and Mars missions, validated with real crew and analog-mission data.

Tools React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Recharts, Google model-viewer, glTF-Transform, Draco, meshoptimizer, Vitest (165 automated tests), Node.js server for the optional online assistant, Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn) for the synthetic data and model training.
